    A Simple and Complete Model Theory for Intensional and Extensional Untyped -Equality

    Michael Gabbay

    Department of Philosophy, Kings College London

    Murdoch Gabbay

    Department of Computer Science, Heriott-Watt University, Edinburgh

    Abstract

    We present a sound and complete model theory for theories of -reduction with or without -expansion. The models of this paper derive from structures of modal logic: we use ternary accessibility relations on ‘possible worlds’ to model the action of intensional and extensional lambda-abstraction in much the same way binary accessibility relations are used to model the box operators of a normal multi-modal logic.

    Keywords: Lambda Calculus, Reduction, Intensional Equality, Extensional Equality, Model Theory, Completeness, Kripke Frames, Possible World Semantics, Modal Logic.

    1 Introduction

    We extend the method of [6] by which we interpret -terms compositionally on ‘possible world’ structures. The simplicity of the structures is striking, moreover, they provide a surprising richness of interpretations of function abstraction and application.

    Our primary goal is to show how the models can diﬀerentiate between extensional and intensional -equality, and provide semantic characterisation (i.e. completeness) theorems for both. We shall then hint at how richer -languages can be interpreted.

    We are very grateful to the input and suggestions of the referees of this journal paper and of its previous incarnation as a conference paper at CiE 2012.

    Vol. 1 No. 2 2014 IFCoLog Journal of Logic and its Applications

    The key idea in this paper is a class of models, presented in Section 2.2, although an important syntactic consideration is required ﬁrst in Section 2.1. These ideas bear some similarity to the reduction models of [18] in that they get us as far as -reduction only. Then, in Section 4 we use the results of the earlier sections to provide a characterisation theorem for -equality (both with and without -equality, i.e. extensional and intensional).

    Definition 2.17

    Remark 2.18

    Deﬁnition 2.17 is not ideal. A semantic characterisation of faithfulness — as a condition on , and — is desirable. We cannot present such a charactersiation in this paper except in the special cases of theories of -equality which we defer until 5.1 of Section 5. In spite of this, the structures characterised by 2.17 are informative because they allow us to break down -abstraction into a quantiﬁcation over worlds with a ternary accessibility relation; the denotations of -terms then become simply sets of worlds. On this analysis the domain of quantiﬁcation for -abstraction — the actual set of denotations of -terms — is , a subset of the set of all possible denotations . This is a common pattern, for example in topological semantics for modal logics and for intuitionistic logic the set of denotations, the analogue of , is the set of all open subsets of the domain rather than the powerset itself. It is then no accident that will reveal further significance: it will be useful later in characterising the diﬀerence between extensional and intensional -calculus (see Remark 3.18). Unlike in the modal case, we oﬀer no general way in this paper of characterising beyond simply saying that it must contain t for each valuation and term t. For a considerably more complex characterisation of in topological terms see [8].

    Remark 3.16

    An extensional frame satisﬁes -expansion. An intensional frame is like an extensional frame except with an additional ‘outer’ application function . We interpret in terms of the outer function and application in terms of the inner function to block -expansion (Deﬁnition 2.13). -expansion will prove useful in constructing models of -equality in Section 4. Other authors have also noted reasons to include -expansion in models [13].

    Remark 3.17

    Given 3.15, we can say that -reduction with -expansion is complete for extensional frames.

    Remark 3.18

    Notice also a crucial purpose served by in the completeness proof. Any subset of a frame is a potential denotation of a -term, and may be seen as listing the subsets that actually are denotations of -terms. We have used this distinction to characterise intensional -reduction.

    We took an (intensional) set of -reductions Γ (in ) and we extended it using to help us interpret (Deﬁnition 2.5 and Theorem 2.8). Then, when we constructed the frame (Deﬁnition 3.5) for Γ we left out of the denotations depending explicitly on . We obtained a frame which is sensitive to all the reductions of Γ, in the original language , but where the interpretation of still depends on which is not mentioned in Γ (Theorem 3.8).

    As we shall see, this provides a simple characterisation of intensional and extensional -abstraction. Abusing notation somewhat: extensional xt is something that maps objects in the domain to t; intensional xt is something maps objects in the domain and also some in a hidden domain to t. Furthermore, the ‘hidden’ objects are the denotations of terms in that require .

    Corollary 4.2 is itself not so signiﬁcant as it only tells us half the story about what these models look like, and does not tell us if there are any non-trivial ones.     5 Faithfulness

    The completeness result 4.15 relates theories to faithful -complete frames. Faithfulness was deﬁned in 2.17 partially syntactically: a faithful frame is one that has a denotation for every -term t.

    It is natural to seek a characterisation of faithfulness that does not require explicit reference to the syntax, i.e. a purely semantic one. Can we provide a description, only in terms of and , of structural properties a frame must have in order that there is an to be the denotation of each -term?     6 Further work

    The methods used here resemble those behind the models of -calculus constructed by Engeler, Meyer, Plotkin and Scott (e.g. in [4, 14] and in [1, §18-19]) which are the basis of graph models.

    The frames presented here have the components , and . Both and have an analogue in graph models, and the diﬀerences between them and their analogues are not of great signiﬁcance: it is not hard to associate each graph model with an equivalent extensional frame (see Remark 2.15). The analogue of in graph models is that denotations are drawn from the powerset of the domain (the analogue of ). The fact that in the models and frames of this paper can be something other than is signiﬁcant. The completeness theorem 3.12 shows this, for it implies that every consistent -theory can be associated with a frame, and yet as shown by Salibra [17] there are -theories for which there are no graph models.

    The models of this paper separate expansion and reduction for both and as distinct semantic properties of a model. Interestingly, -reduction and -expansion are natural features of the models (there is independent evidence that this is natural [13]). -expansion arises from -abstraction and application being deﬁned over the same underlying function . If we use two underlying functions and instead, where , so that abstracts over and application applies , then we obtain models free from -expansion.

    We could also reverse this ‘trick’ so that abstracts over the and application applies , and thus obtain models free from -reduction. This may sound perverse but recall that meta-programming languages — languages that can suspend their own evaluation and/or quote their own syntax — are devoted to switching oﬀ -reduction in a controlled manner, and the connections to modal logic have already been noted, where possible worlds correspond to deeper or shallower levels of suspension or quoting (see MetaML [15] and CMTT [16, 9]). This suggests the possibility of models for a variety of interacting -operators over a hierarchy of underlying application relations.

    Finally, further work is needed in improving the semantic characterisations, in terms of and , of frames that are Γ-sensitive for interesting Γ. For example, can we provide a helpful semantic characterisation of theories that contain the schema of -reduction? We can do it in terms of by specifying that, for any , , but it would also be interesting to look for conditions on and alone that correspond to this, independently of .
